questions.prompt: Why is a malicious Security Support Provider both persistence and credential theft?
options: The DLL loads into lsass.exe at boot and, because SSPs participate in authentication, can observe plaintext credentials as users log on
It steals certificates rather than passwords
It only captures credentials for one session
questions.explanation: Registering an SSP places attacker code inside the process that handles authentication -- surviving reboot and capturing credentials without needing to dump LSASS memory.

questions.prompt: What makes the Security Packages value unusually easy to audit?
options: It is automatically compared against a Microsoft baseline
The known-good list is short and stable (kerberos, msv1_0, schannel, wdigest, tspkg, pku2u, negoexts, cloudap), so anything outside it is immediately investigable
It cannot be modified without a reboot
It is protected by Tamper Protection
questions.explanation: Unlike artifacts requiring extensive baselining, this value has a short expected list that varies only slightly by Windows version and join state.

questions.prompt: Why will a registry-only check miss the Mimikatz misc::memssp variant?
options: It writes to HKCU instead of HKLM
It injects an SSP directly into running LSASS memory with no registry modification, so it exists only until reboot
It disables the registry service entirely
questions.explanation: The memory-only variant leaves no persistent registry artifact -- detecting it requires memory analysis or an image-load event showing an unexpected DLL entering lsass.exe.

questions.prompt: How does LSA Protection (RunAsPPL) block both SSP variants?
options: It disables the Security Packages value entirely
It makes LSASS a Protected Process Light that will only load signed modules, so an unsigned SSP DLL cannot load regardless of registry state
It encrypts all credentials in memory
It prevents any DLL from loading into LSASS
questions.explanation: Because the protection enforces signature requirements on loaded modules, both the registry-registered and memory-injected unsigned variants fail -- generating a CodeIntegrity 3033 event when they do.
